name: Postfix
summary: A modular mail transfer agent that separates SMTP admission and message cleanup from address resolution, bounded queue scheduling, transport delivery, and retry or bounce handling.

features.name: Multi-stage message admission and cleanup
features.description: Postfix accepts network mail through smtpd and local submissions through pickup or sendmail/postdrop, then sends sender, recipients, and content to cleanup. cleanup canonicalizes the message and writes one queue file to the incoming queue before notifying the queue manager.
benefits: Separates SMTP protocol handling from queue-file creation
Provides one normalization boundary for network and local submissions
Lets admission checks and lightweight content inspection occur before scheduling
costs: Each handoff adds IPC, configuration, and observable failure boundaries
Ingress validation does not establish successful downstream delivery
A burst of accepted mail can compete for disk and queue-manager attention

features.name: Address rewriting and transport resolution boundary
features.description: The trivial-rewrite service transforms addresses to standard form and resolves recipients to a transport, next hop, recipient, and flags. cleanup performs message-level canonical and alias transformations while trivial-rewrite supplies the routing result used by delivery scheduling.
benefits: Keeps address policy and destination selection reusable across delivery paths
Reduces lookup-table variation through canonical address form
Makes transport selection explicit before a delivery agent is invoked
costs: Routing behavior is distributed across configuration tables and service boundaries
A syntactically accepted address can still resolve to an unavailable destination
Reload timing and lookup failures affect future queue decisions

features.name: Bounded active queue and deferred retry scheduler
features.description: The qmgr service maintains incoming, active, and deferred queue state. The active queue is a limited window on larger queues, delivery is delegated to transport-specific agents, and temporary failures are retried with delayed scheduling and backoff. Hold suspends delivery until release; corrupt isolates unreadable queue files for inspection. Per-recipient bounce, defer, and trace records are distinct from queue-file membership.
benefits: Bounds scheduler working state under large backlogs
Separates newly queued work from delayed failures
Allows transport-specific concurrency and delivery policies
costs: Backlog age and retry delay become part of delivery behavior
A shared queue manager can compete with front-end processes for disk access
Flushing deferred work too aggressively can reduce delivery performance

features.name: Transport delivery agents and per-recipient status
features.description: qmgr requests delivery through distinct smtp, lmtp, local, virtual, pipe, discard, or error agents. Delivery agents report completion or a request to retry, allowing queue state and recipient status to advance independently for a message with multiple recipients.
benefits: Supports multiple local, remote, and integration delivery mechanisms
Keeps transport-specific protocol behavior outside queue scheduling
Allows success, temporary failure, permanent failure, and bounce paths to be represented
costs: The delivery result depends on agent, destination, and configuration semantics
Partial recipient progress complicates message lifecycle and status reporting
External commands and remote transports widen the failure surface

features.name: Process privilege and SMTP authentication boundaries
features.description: Postfix runs many services under master process supervision and supports separate SASL implementations for SMTP authentication, including a Dovecot SASL integration. Service-specific process and privilege boundaries, optional chrooting, TLS policy, and access controls constrain exposure at the network and delivery edges.
benefits: Limits the blast radius of protocol-facing or lookup-facing code
Separates SMTP authentication mechanism selection from message routing
Provides configurable TLS and access-control enforcement points
costs: Privilege, chroot, TLS, and SASL configuration must be mutually compatible
Authentication success still does not imply message delivery success
Security policy is spread across service definitions, lookup tables, and protocol settings

mathematical_views.model: Message admission and delivery state machine
mathematical_views.question: How does a message move from SMTP or local admission through cleanup, queueing, routing, delivery, retry, bounce, or completion?
assumptions: A message has distinct admission, normalized, queued, active, delivered, deferred, bounced, and terminal states
A message with multiple recipients may have different recipient outcomes at the same time
SMTP acceptance is modeled as an ingress transition and not as proof of final delivery
The view abstracts queue-file record encoding and wire-level SMTP commands

mathematical_views.question: How do active-queue bounds, transport concurrency, destination status, delayed retries, and deferred scans constrain delivery throughput?
assumptions: Queue files are work items and active membership is a bounded scheduling window
Transport and destination limits are resource constraints rather than protocol guarantees
Temporary delivery failures schedule future transitions with a backoff policy
Let A be active messages and M the configured active-message bound: |A| <= M limits scheduler membership, not total queued bytes or total process memory
If sustained accepted arrival exceeds completed delivery, backlog can grow despite a bounded active window; storage capacity and upstream admission still matter
Hold requires an administrative release transition, and corrupt files do not represent successful delivery
The model does not claim fairness or latency bounds for arbitrary configuration

mathematical_views.question: Which Postfix services exchange message, routing, authentication, and delivery state, and where are privilege or protocol trust boundaries placed?
assumptions: Master, smtpd, cleanup, trivial-rewrite, qmgr, delivery agents, and SASL services are vertices
IPC and queue-file edges represent explicit handoffs of bounded state
Privilege and chroot settings are modeled as deployment-dependent boundary labels
The graph distinguishes the SMTP protocol implementation from the Postfix services that host it

benefits: Protocol admission and message normalization have explicit boundaries
costs: IPC and disk handoffs create additional operational failure points

benefits: Routing policy can be composed from reusable lookup and transport rules
costs: Distributed configuration makes routing behavior harder to reason about

benefits: Active work is bounded while failed work remains retryable
costs: Backoff and queue contention trade immediate latency against system stability

benefits: Delivery mechanisms can evolve independently of queue admission
costs: Per-transport and per-recipient outcomes enlarge failure-state space

benefits: Network-facing and delivery-facing components can run with constrained trust
costs: Security configuration and cross-service authentication integration require careful coordination

relations.notes: Postfix's SASL documentation and fixed source explicitly cover Dovecot as an optional SASL authentication provider; the relation is a configured integration boundary, not a universal Postfix dependency.
